In essence, we now have the ability to optimally place materials at the micro level so as to tailor their effective material properties at the meso and macro scale levels. This concept of material optimization has a natural fit in the additive manufacture of fiber-reinforced composites. In addition to the high strength to weight ratio, fiber-reinforced polymer composites offer ex- ceptionalpropertiessuchashighdurability,stiffness,damping,flexuralstrength,andresistancetocorrosion, wear, impact, and fire [1]. Now optimal fiber placement and orientation in composite structures enabled by advanced manufacturing can significantly increase the structure’s mechanical performance. The interested reader is referred to [2], for a review on additively manufactured composite structures. Inmanyadvancedmanufacturingprocesses,astructure’sComputerAidedDesign(CAD)modelissliced into planar layers. The layers are covered by machine toolpaths, e.g., G-code that is used to drive their Computer Numerical Control (CNC) additive manufacturing process. However, robotic systems are not constrained by this planar layer-by-layer approach [3]. Indeed, parts can still be built layer-by-layer, but these layers need not to be planar, i.e., we can build a three-dimensional structure surface-by-surface. AFPmachinescanplaceandsteerthefibertowsonsurfacesallowingthefiberangle orientationandhencethematerialproperties,tocontinuouslyvary. Duetothismaterialheterogeneity,such structures are called Variable Stiffness (VS) composites. Most VS composite cylinders vary the orientation in a piece-wise linear manner, e.g., [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14]. The resulting cylinders have their fibers aligned to, e.g., resist buckling loads. Blom et al. [15] define toolpaths for composite conical structures that allow them to extract the fiber orientation and enforce constraints with respect to overlaps and local curvature. The authors in [16] propose material tailoring schemes for elliptical cylinders, wherein the ellipse’s radius of curvature is used to define the fiber angle orientation based on the buckling analyses of composite circu- lar cylinders. Khani et al. [11] optimize circular and elliptical cylinders for maximum buckling load with strength constraints. In the first step of this method, optimal lamination parameters are obtained. Then in a post-processing step, fiber paths with limited curvature are constructed by using Quadratic Constrained Quadratic Programming, a Genetic Algorithm, and the stream function theory. Khani et al. [13] subse- quently use this approach to study the presence of longitudinal stiffeners on composite cylindrical shells. In [12], to reduce computational expense, surrogate modeling combined with a Genetic Algorithm is used to maximize the buckling load of VS composite cylinders. This work was extended to multiple buckling loads in [14] and elliptical cylinders in [17].
